title: Infant Skin Characteristics
subtitle: Skin
content: Anatomical and physiological properties of infant skin compared to adults.
notes: Thin and transparent; thickness in children <3 years is 1.5–3 times less than in adults
Fair/light due to reduced melanocyte function
Smooth, delicate, and soft, containing up to 80% water
Loose epidermal structure with cells relatively far apart, making it sensitive, vulnerable, and prone to desquamation
Weak dermo-epidermal junction (poorly developed anchoring fibers) predisposes to epidermal detachment and bullae formation
Neutral skin pH results in poor antibacterial protection

title: Skin Appendages: Glands, Hair, and Nails
subtitle: Skin
content: Developmental milestones and functional characteristics of cutaneous appendages in newborns, children, and adolescents.
notes: Sebaceous glands function in utero to produce vernix caseosa, which protects fetal skin from amniotic fluid and eases passage through the birth canal
Sebaceous gland activity peaks in puberty, where occlusion by epithelial plugs leads to acne
Sweat gland function is decreased during the first 3–4 months due to underdeveloped, occluded excretory ducts; sweating starts at 3–4 weeks at higher threshold temperatures and matures by 7–8 years
Apocrine sweat glands begin functioning in puberty
Newborns are covered in lanugo (more prominent in premature infants), have poorly developed eyebrows/eyelashes, and replace primary scalp hair within the first 6 months
Nails reach the fingertips in term infants; a growth delay in the first 3 days creates a 'physiological line' that reaches the free edge by the 3rd month

title: Primary Skin Lesions
subtitle: Skin
content: Initial pathological changes presenting on previously unaltered skin.
notes: Spots (flat color changes): Inflammatory spots blanch on pressure (roseola ≤ 5 mm, macula 6–20 mm, erythema > 20 mm); non-inflammatory spots do not blanch (nevus, hemangioma, petechiae, purpura 2–5 mm, ecchymosis > 5 mm)
Elevated solid lesions: Papules (palpable, discrete, < 1 cm), plaques (> 1 cm), nodules (solid or cystic, 1–2 cm), and wheals (irregular, elevated, edematous areas)
Fluid-filled lesions: Pustules (purulent content), vesicles (< 1 cm, serous/hemorrhagic fluid), and bullae (> 1 cm)
Pigment and vascular changes: Hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, and telangiectasia (dilated superficial blood vessel)

title: Secondary Skin Lesions and Dermographism
subtitle: Skin
content: Evolved modifications of primary lesions and mechanical skin reactivity.
notes: Surface loss/breaks: Excoriation (linear erosion from scratching), erosion (superficial focal epidermal loss), ulceration (loss extending into dermis), and fissure (deep split into dermis)

Surface accumulations and thickening: Scale (desiccated keratinized flakes), crust (dried serum, blood, sebum, or pus), lichenification (thickening with exaggerated markings from chronic inflammation), and scar (fibrous tissue replacement)
Dermographism: 'Writing on the skin' via firm stroking; normally turns white, then red, and is transient

title: Nail and Hair Pathologies
subtitle: Skin
content: Clinical signs associated with abnormal nail plate and hair growth.
notes: Nail changes: Thimble symptom (pitting), convex/watch-glass nails, koilonychia (spoon nails linked to iron deficiency), leukonychia (white spots/streaks), and onychophagia (nail-biting)
Hair changes: Alopecia (hair loss) and hypertrichosis (excessive hair growth)

title: Pediatric Skeletal System: General, Skull, Spine, and Chest
subtitle: Bones
content: Developmental features, fontanelle closure timelines, spinal curves, and thoracic deformities in children.
notes: Children's bones are more elastic with a thick periosteum, predisposing them to rapidly healing 'greenstick' (subperiosteal) fractures
All newborn bones contain red bone marrow for hematopoiesis (restricted to flat/short bones and long bone epiphyses in adults)
Skull has fontanelles and sutures allowing molding during birth and brain growth; neurocranium volume greatly exceeds viscerocranium
Large (anterior) fontanelle (coronal/sagittal intersection, up to 3x3 cm) closes by 1–1.5 years; small (posterior) fontanelle (occipital/parietal) is closed at birth or by 1–2 months

Newborn spine is arch-shaped; physiological curves develop sequentially: cervical lordosis (2–3 months, lifting head), thoracic kyphosis (sitting), and lumbar lordosis/sacral kyphosis (9–12 months, standing/walking)
Pediatric chest has horizontal ribs and a greater anteroposterior than transverse diameter; common deformities include pectus excavatum (koilosternia) and pectus carinatum (chicken/keeled breast)

title: Pediatric Dentition
subtitle: Bones
content: Timelines and calculation formulas for deciduous and permanent tooth eruption.
notes: Primary (milk) tooth eruption begins at 5–7 months (may cause fever, sleep disturbance, diarrhea) and reaches 20 teeth by 2 years
Formula for expected number of milk teeth: X = n - 4 (where n = age in months)
Replacement of milk teeth with permanent teeth starts around 5 years
Formula for expected number of permanent teeth: X = 4n - 20 (where n = age in years)
